Foxfish (Bodianus frenchii) attains a maximum total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the genus within temperate Australian reefs. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this length reaches approximately 1300 grams [Wwi = approximately 1300 grams], a figure derived from length-weight relationships established for this species. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty, occurring at a length of 24.5 cm [Lp = 24.5 cm], is far more modest at 207 grams [Wwp = 207 grams], indicating that a substantial proportion of somatic growth is deferred until after the onset of reproductive maturity. This growth pattern, in which individuals more than double their length after puberty, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises early reproduction while continuing to increase body size, a pattern also observed in several other labrid fishes occupying similar rocky reef habitats.

Neonatal body mass in Bodianus frenchii is remarkably small, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerging from pelagic eggs that measure approximately 570 micrometres in diameter. The wet weight at birth, calculated from egg dimensions and assuming spherical geometry, is estimated at 0.000097 grams [Wwb = 0.000097 grams]. These tiny prolarvae are entirely lecithotrophic at eclosion, relying on endogenous yolk reserves during the early endotrophic phase that precedes the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to first feeding typically occurs within a few days following yolk absorption, after which the free-swimming larva enters a planktonic phase of several weeks. The extreme disparity between birth mass and adult mass in this species, spanning nearly seven orders of magnitude, underscores the intensity of the growth trajectory required to reach the ultimate body size recorded for adult individuals.

Longevity data for Foxfish, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith readings conducted at a consistent water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], indicate that maximum lifespan is approximately 80 years [am = approximately 80 years]. This exceptional longevity places Bodianus frenchii among the longest-lived labrids known from southern Australian waters, a remarkable feat for a species that reaches puberty at a relatively modest size. The 80-year lifespan is likely linked to the species' slow growth rate following sexual maturation, as well as the relatively stable thermal environment it inhabits. At the controlled temperature of 18 °C, metabolic rates are moderate, which may contribute to reduced oxidative damage and delayed senescence, though direct physiological data on age-related decline in this species remain limited to a handful of longitudinal field studies.

The onset of vitellogenesis and eventual first spawning in Bodianus frenchii occurs only after individuals have attained a sufficient body size to support the energetic demands of gamete production. The total length at puberty has been recorded at 24.5 cm [Lp = 24.5 cm], corresponding to a wet weight of 207 grams [Wwp = 207 grams] at that developmental milestone. This size threshold is likely linked to habitat acquisition, as larger individuals are better able to defend feeding territories on the rocky reefs they inhabit. The gonadosomatic index increases markedly once this size is surpassed, with spawning aggregations forming during the austral summer months. Comparative data from other labrids suggest that the size at first reproduction is shaped by a trade-off between the survival benefits of continued growth and the fitness advantages of early reproductive output.

One of the most striking demographic features of the Foxfish is its longevity, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of 80 years [am = 80 years] in the wild under the ambient thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Such an extended life span is unusual among reef fishes of its maximum size of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], as most temperate labrids of comparable ultimate total length typically live for two to three decades at most. The ultimate wet weight of 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams] is attained gradually over many decades, with growth curves indicating a deceleration in length increase after the onset of maturity. The combination of a modest adult weight and an extraordinarily long life span suggests that Bodianus frenchii invests heavily in somatic maintenance and survival rather than in rapid reproduction, a life-history strategy that aligns well with the stable, low-predation environment of its subtidal reef habitat.
